title: The Unique Games Conjecture and optimal approximation thresholds
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Proves Khot's Unique Games Conjecture: Goemans-Williamson's 0.878 for Max-Cut and the factor 2 for Vertex Cover are now unconditionally the best ratios any polynomial-time algorithm can guarantee on worst-case inputs (unless P=NP). Separate direct reductions also give constant-factor hardness for Min-UnCut and directed feedback vertex set.
constructive: yes (deterministic poly-time reductions from 3SAT; alphabet F_2^s with s fixed by eps,delta)
explicit_constants: none useful: alphabet size and polynomial degree depend on eps,delta and are not tabulated; output instances are astronomically large for interesting eps
opportunity: No code gets faster. What changes is the status of claims: the GW SDP rounding and the 2-approximation for Vertex Cover are provably optimal in the worst case, assuming only P!=NP. A non-obvious channel is quantum optimization. A QAOA or annealer algorithm that guaranteed better than 0.8786 on every graph would now imply NP in BQP, with no UGC assumption. Benchmarking groups should therefore frame advantage claims as instance-specific or average-case.
targets: Qiskit Optimization / OpenQAOA Max-Cut advantage literature
Williamson-Shmoys approximation-algorithms curriculum (UGC-conditional results become unconditional)
first_step: Write a short note for quantum-optimization benchmarking groups: a worst-case ratio above alpha_GW, or below 2 for VC, now implies NP in BQP, so compare against GW+local search on concrete instance families instead.
caveats: Worst-case only. Practitioners already used heuristics and UGC was widely assumed true, so the marginal change in practice is small. The reductions are too large to generate useful hard benchmark instances.

title: Exact derandomization of logarithmic space: L=RL=BPL
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Every randomized log-space polynomial-time algorithm can be simulated deterministically in log space and polynomial time.
constructive: yes (explicit compiler emitting deterministic machine and bounds K,H,c)
explicit_constants: explicit but huge: time constant H=2^{(u+100)^2}(q_D+1) with u >= source transition-table bit length; exponent c=2S+1 source-dependent
opportunity: None in practice. The simulation is white-box: it inverts (I-S) on the machine's configuration graph and does not construct a pseudorandom generator or hitting set for read-once branching programs. It therefore cannot replace Nisan/INW generators in streaming or sketch derandomization, which practical sketches avoid anyway by using k-wise independent hashing. The compiler constants (2^{(u+100)^2}) are astronomical.
caveats: Theory landmark only. A practical channel would need a black-box PRG or hitting set, which this proof does not give.

title: Quasipolynomial algorithms for mean-payoff, stochastic and parity games
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Deterministic algorithms decide who wins mean-payoff games, mean-payoff parity games and turn-based stochastic mean-payoff games (including Condon's simple stochastic games) in 2^{O(log^2 L)} time, even with huge binary-encoded weights and probabilities.
constructive: yes (fully specified recursive procedure Label(A,D,a,b) with exact integer/rational arithmetic; randomized variant has poly-time certificate check)
explicit_constants: partly explicit: base case D<4096, factors 4/3, 8/5, rho=32/25; call bound (H+1)(B0+1)(1+Hs)^{B0} with s=2048n+3, B0~log_{1.28}(n^2); absolute C not tabulated
opportunity: This is the only fully specified, implementable exact algorithm in the batch whose constants are not astronomical by construction. It is also the first deterministic quasipolynomial algorithm for simple stochastic games and binary-weight mean-payoff games. Quantitative verification and synthesis tools solve these games with value iteration or strategy iteration, which have exponential worst cases (Friedmann-type instances). An empirical test would show whether the new recursion is a useful robust fallback. The appendix's Lean-checked counterexample to Truffet's claimed strongly polynomial tropical LP rule is a small side redirect.
targets: mean-payoff/energy game solvers (Brim et al. value iteration, Bjorklund-Vorobyov strategy improvement)
first_step: Implement Procedure Label (deterministic paper, Sec. 4) in exact arithmetic and run it against Zielonka/strategy-improvement on Friedmann lower-bound families and SYNTCOMP parity->mean-payoff reductions with large weights.
caveats: The worst-case call bound is enormous even at n=100 (on the order of 10^300). Quasipolynomial parity algorithms (Calude et al.) were empirically slower than Zielonka in Oink. The deterministic paper is not Lean-formalized (the randomized one is). The binary-weight advantage matters only for huge weights.

title: Perfect completeness for 2-to-1 games
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: It is NP-hard to tell fully satisfiable 2-to-1 label-cover games from games where only a small fraction of constraints can be satisfied.
constructive: yes (poly-time reduction from 3SAT)
explicit_constants: alphabet q(delta) and polynomial degree depend on delta, not tabulated
opportunity: None. This is an intermediate PCP/hardness tool, mainly feeding hardness of coloring results such as 106, with no practitioner-facing decision.
caveats: Pure complexity theory.

title: Hardness of coloring three-colorable graphs
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Coloring a 3-colorable graph with any fixed number of colors is NP-hard, and finding an independent set of size delta*n in such graphs is NP-hard too.
constructive: yes (poly-time reduction)
explicit_constants: degree/constants depend on delta, not tabulated
opportunity: No applied change. Graph-coloring users (register allocation, timetabling, frequency assignment) already rely on heuristics and exact solvers, and nobody relied on a constant-color guarantee for 3-colorable inputs. The result redirects only theoretical work on O(1)-coloring algorithms.
caveats: Theory redirect only. The hard instances from the reduction are not usable benchmarks.

title: Matrix multiplication with exponent at most 9/4
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Proves that n x n complex matrices can be multiplied with O(n^{9/4+eps}) arithmetic operations, down from about n^2.371. Companion papers give omega<2.371055 over every field and better rectangular exponents.
constructive: no for 9/4: existence via Strassen's asymptotic-spectrum duality; the final algorithm takes 'a fixed integer u and an exact rank decomposition of T_u of length r<u^{9/4+delta}' supplied by the definition of omega, so u and the decomposition are never computed. Companion 2.371 paper uses laser-method extraction with N->infinity strand counts.
explicit_constants: none: paper states 'its proof does not specify a competitive finite matrix size'; 2.371 paper states 'do not give bit-complexity or practical crossover estimates'; coefficients over C (algebraic by Nullstellensatz)
opportunity: No implementation opportunity. The prior claim to 'add a kernel to FLINT nmod_mat_mul' is wrong on every count. (1) The 9/4 proof is non-constructive: it bounds all spectral points and never exhibits a bilinear algorithm. (2) Even the constructive laser-method family (Coppersmith-Winograd and descendants) has never been implemented because its crossover is astronomical. (3) Degeneration-based schemes need interpolation over many eps values and are numerically unstable. (4) FLINT, like every production library, uses Strassen-Winograd above a crossover of a few hundred plus BLAS-backed classical multiplication. The only real-world touchpoint is cost models that quote 'omega=2.37' (for example asymptotic columns in multivariate/lattice crypto estimators). These should not switch to 9/4, because conservative estimators already use omega=2 (MQEstimator default w=2).
caveats: Huge theoretical significance (Lean-formalized), zero practical speedup at any size. Do not propagate it into crypto security estimates as a 'real' cost exponent.
evidence: /root/openai-math/preprints/Matrix-Multiplication-Nine-Fourths-October-2-2026/build/paper.tex (thm:main, lem:growth, proof of thm:main, Remark after it)

title: A cubic permanent-determinant lower bound
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Writing the m x m permanent as a determinant of affine-linear entries, even approximately (border sense), needs matrix size at least c*m^3.
constructive: n/a (lower bound)
opportunity: None. This is algebraic complexity (VP vs VNP / GCT) with no algorithmic consequence for computing permanents. Practical permanent and hafnian codes (Ryser/Glynn, The Walrus) are unaffected.
caveats: Pure lower bound.

title: Integer multiplication below n log n
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Two n-bit integers can be multiplied on a multitape Turing machine in O(n (log n)^{1-kappa}) time with kappa=2^-182, disproving Schonhage-Strassen's n log n optimality conjecture in that model.
constructive: yes in principle (one fixed multitape TM) but only meaningful asymptotically
explicit_constants: explicit and absurd: kappa=2^-182; d=floor(b^{2^-75}) with b=ceil(log2 n), so the multidimensional structure needs d>=2, i.e. n>=2^(2^(2^75)); paper says 'constants and thresholds in the construction are extremely large'
opportunity: None. The claimed 'GMP/OpenSSL/CPython' opportunity is baseless. The saving factor is (lg n)^{2^-182}: even at n=2^(2^64) bits it is 1+O(10^-53). The construction's parameter d only exceeds 1 once n>=2^(2^(2^75)). The model is a multitape TM, not a word RAM. In practice, CPython uses Karatsuba, OpenSSL BN uses Karatsuba/Comba at 2-16 kbit crypto sizes, and GMP uses Toom-Cook and Schonhage-Strassen FFT. Even the O(n log n) Harvey-van der Hoeven algorithm it improves is itself galactic.
caveats: Not Lean-formalized. The 470KB proof is unreviewed and the claim is extraordinary (confidence 2). Even if true, it has no effect on any software.

title: Optimal-order randomized k-server on arbitrary metrics
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: There is a randomized online policy for moving k servers to requests whose expected cost is O(log^2 k) times the offline optimum on any metric. This matches the known worst-case lower bound.
constructive: partial: main paper is existential ('no computational-efficiency claim'); companion gives a uniform algorithm via LP tables over bounded request words with delayed activation
explicit_constants: multiplicative C=4(2a+1) (absolute, partly explicit, e.g. C=288 in travel lemma); additive movement constant 'finite, instance-dependent, may be enormous'
opportunity: None. The computable version solves finite LPs over all bounded request words and serves an 'enormous initial number' of requests with a fixed fallback before activating, so the additive loss is unbounded in practice. Caching and dispatch systems use LRU/ARC-type or problem-specific heuristics. Coester-Cosson 2026 is already polynomial-time with O(log^2 k log n).
caveats: Theory resolution of the randomized k-server question. Not a deployable policy.

title: One-sample matroid prophet inequalities against an almighty adversary
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: With one past sample per item and any matroid constraint, an online selection rule earns a constant fraction of the offline optimum, even against an adversary who sees everything.
constructive: partial: measurable rule, explicitly 'no running-time or polynomial independence-oracle guarantee'
opportunity: None. A 2^-310 guarantee is meaningless for posted pricing, ad allocation or online hiring, which use rules with 1/2 or 1/e-type guarantees under weaker adversaries, and the rule has no efficiency guarantee.
caveats: Theoretical constant-vs-loglog separation only.

title: Beyond the square-root exponent for depth-three circuits
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: An explicit polynomial-time language needs 2^{omega(sqrt n)} gates in depth-3 OR-AND-OR circuits.
constructive: n/a (lower bound, explicit language)
opportunity: None. This is circuit-complexity progress with no applied channel.
caveats: Pure.

title: Approximate counting and entropy of perfect matchings
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Gives a randomized polynomial-time (1+eps)-approximate counter of perfect matchings in any graph, the first for non-bipartite graphs. It extends to counting subgraphs with prescribed degrees and matchings of fixed size. A companion proves the Anari-Oveis Gharan-Vinzant entropy conjecture and a deterministic 512^n-factor counter.
constructive: yes (explicit annealing + replicated-tier product chain; deterministic subgradient algorithm in companion)
explicit_constants: explicit but galactic: replica count q=32L with L=(10^4 N D)^100 (eq:energy-constants, eq:ladder-parameters); 'constants chosen for transparent estimates rather than practical efficiency'; companion deterministic factor 512^n
opportunity: No usable code: the polynomial has degree in the hundreds. The non-obvious channel is quantum. Gaussian boson sampling 'graph applications' (Bradler et al. 2018, 'GBS for perfect matchings of arbitrary graphs'; Xanadu application stacks) motivate quantum speedups for estimating perfect-matching counts of general graphs. A classical FPRAS for unweighted general graphs removes any complexity-theoretic advantage claim for that task. GBS sampling-hardness arguments are untouched, since they rest on complex or general hafnians and exact sampling. The theory also pairs with 131 and 115 for degree-constrained null models.
targets: Strawberry Fields / The Walrus GBS application literature (perfect-matching counting, graph similarity)
first_step: Write a short note for the GBS applications community: approximate counting of perfect matchings in unweighted general graphs is classically in FPRAS, so GBS application claims must target weighted or complex hafnians or exact-sampling tasks.
caveats: Galactic polynomial, so practitioners will still use heuristics or exact Pfaffian methods (planar molecules/dimers). The FPRAS covers simple unweighted graphs; nonnegative weighted hafnians are only covered with the weak 512^n deterministic factor.
evidence: /root/openai-math/preprints/A-Fully-Polynomial-Randomized-Approximation-Scheme-for-Perfect-Matchings-in-General-Graphs-September-23-2026/build/main.tex (thm:main l.132, eq:energy-constants l.1595, eq:ladder-parameters l.2249, sec. complexity l.2843-3080, cor:prescribed-degree l.3100)

title: Approximate counting of common integer polymatroid bases
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Gives a randomized polynomial-time approximate counter for objects that are simultaneously bases of two matroids, or integer bases of two polymatroids with huge capacities, using only rank or independence oracles.
constructive: yes (annealing + Lorentzian-signature transport chain)
explicit_constants: explicit but galactic: U=N^61000 with N>=10^10 (polymatroid paper); N_av=ceil(10^10 (L+1) n^14/eta^2) (matroid paper); 'large fixed exponents'
opportunity: None practical. The natural special cases are either already exact (arborescences via the matrix-tree theorem) or already covered (bipartite matchings via JSV), and exponents like N^61000 rule out implementation.
caveats: Theory resolution of a well-known counting question.

title: Sampling and counting contingency tables with arbitrary margins
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Gives polynomial-time uniform sampling (exact and approximate) of nonnegative integer matrices with given row and column sums, and approximate counting when each cell also has an upper bound (including structural zeros).
constructive: yes (explicit padded small-cell chain + dense lattice-walk completion + GLMP exact correction)
explicit_constants: explicit and galactic: d=10+(m+1)(n+1), padding L=d^12, threshold U=d^20, chain length T=d^200 (k+b)^2, exact-correction tabulation 2^{500db}; even a 2x2 table gives d=19, T~10^256 steps. Cell-bounded FPRAS: H=O(L^11 eps^-2), 'deliberately generous'
opportunity: The prior mapping 'contingency tables -> statistics software' is mis-targeted. Fisher's exact test and R fisher.test(simulate.p.value=TRUE) need the hypergeometric law on tables, not the uniform law, and Patefield's r2dtable already samples it exactly and fast. Uniform tables matter for the Diaconis-Efron uniform test, for counting tables (Chen-Diaconis-Holmes-Liu sequential importance sampling), and for microcanonical null models of weighted bipartite and multigraph networks (vegan permatfull/permatswap fixed-fixed models, curveball/swap MCMC). There the new result proves the problem is in P but does not certify the swap or Diaconis-Gangolli chains people actually run, and its sampler is unusable. A follow-on research question is whether its padding/small-cell decomposition yields a practical sampler or a mixing proof for the standard chain.
targets: R vegan permatswap/permatfull (quantitative fixed-margin null models)
first_step: Pose the research question of whether the transversal/padding chain analysis yields an O(poly) mixing bound for the standard 2x2 +/-1 swap chain on integer tables, which would certify existing vegan/ecology practice the way 131 certifies edge switches.
caveats: The degree-200 polynomial is unusable. The result does not apply to the hypergeometric conditional law used by exact tests. The 0/1 case was already covered by JSV 2004.

title: Uniform black-box noncommutative identity testing across characteristics
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Gives one explicit tuple of rational matrices of size about 2ns^2 such that every nonzero noncommutative formula of size s in n variables evaluates to a nonzero matrix there. Zero-testing such expressions thus needs a single deterministic evaluation.
constructive: yes (explicit deterministic construction, poly bit time)
explicit_constants: explicit and moderate: d<=2ns^2 (char 0), entries O(log(ns)+ns^2 log n) bits; char p version dimension O(n^3 s^6)
opportunity: This is a small but real deterministic zero-test for noncommutative expressions given as formulas, where symbolic expansion can blow up exponentially. It could be added to noncommutative computer-algebra packages as a certificate-producing alternative to random matrix evaluation. Demand is niche, because randomized evaluation with Amitsur-Levitzki-size random matrices already works with negligible error.
first_step: Prototype the char-0 tuple (One-Rational-Matrix-Hitting-Point construction.tex) in SageMath for small n,s and compare cost against random-matrix testing.
caveats: Low demand for deterministic NC-PIT. Rational matrices of dimension 2ns^2 with roughly ns^2-bit entries get heavy for s beyond tens.

title: Uniform sparsest cut: hardness and semidefinite gaps
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Approximating uniform sparsest cut within any constant factor is NP-hard. The ARV semidefinite relaxation's sqrt(log n) guarantee is essentially tight (gap sqrt(log n)/(loglog n)^3).
constructive: partial: hardness reduction explicit; integrality-gap sequence existential along n->infinity
explicit_constants: none useful (gap constant c unspecified, only along a sequence)
opportunity: No practitioner impact. Graph-partitioning tools (METIS, KaHIP, Scotch) and spectral clustering are heuristic and do not use ARV SDPs. Removing the UGC/SSE assumption from constant-factor hardness changes nothing they do.
caveats: Theory redirect only. The Lean scope covers the integrality gap and not the hardness theorem.

title: Bin packing and unbounded configuration-LP gaps
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Disproves the Modified Integer Round-Up Conjecture: some bin-packing instances need more bins than the Gilmore-Gomory configuration LP value plus any fixed constant. It is also NP-hard to pack within OPT+c bins for any fixed c, even when every item exceeds 1/6.
constructive: yes (explicit reduction from vertex cover; gap instance built from K4 by a finite deterministic procedure)
explicit_constants: explicit and astronomical: P0=100^11, K=25(c+1)(1+5P0), d>=max(72K,120K/rho) (~2.4e27 for c=1), competing trees with 2d-1 phases of doubling levels, R=100(P+nK+1), denominators [100(D*+1)]^L 3^n; item count far beyond physical
opportunity: This settles a question the cutting-stock/OR community has pursued computationally for decades. Kartak, Ripatti, Scheithauer and Kurz enumerated non-IRUP instances and found gaps only slightly above 1. MIRUP is false, but every counterexample from this construction is astronomically large, so the empirical rule 'gap < 2 on real instances' and the use of ceil(LP) as a lower bound in branch-and-price/arc-flow solvers are unaffected. The actions are to update textbooks and surveys (the Williamson-Shmoys open problem is closed conditionally on P!=NP) and to stop small-instance searches aimed at refuting MIRUP while redirecting them to the smallest instance with gap >=2. The construction gives no usable benchmark instances.
targets: cutting-stock/bin-packing research community (Scheithauer, Kartak, Rietz, Kurz)
Hoberg-Rothvoss O(log OPT) additive algorithm line
first_step: Send the cutting-stock community a short note: MIRUP is false with integral LP value, but witnesses are astronomically large, so the open practical question is the smallest instance with gap >=2.
caveats: Galactic instances, so no benchmark use. Hardness is worst-case, and real solvers run exactly via branch-and-price. It does not give a log-OPT lower bound matching Hoberg-Rothvoss.

title: The Courtade-Kumar and Hellinger conjectures
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Among all one-bit summaries of n uniform random bits, a single coordinate retains the most mutual information about a noisy (bit-flipped) copy of the input: I(f(X);Y) <= 1-h(eps). A Hellinger-distance analogue holds for every output bias.
constructive: n/a (sharp inequality); proofs include finite exact-arithmetic certificates
explicit_constants: explicit and sharp: 1-h2(eps) bits, equality for dictators; bias-refined curve psi(|rho| psi^-1(H(m)))
opportunity: This is a closed-form, sharp converse that engineers can cite for one-bit summaries of noisy binary data (remote source coding with a one-bit compressor, one-bit feedback, information-bottleneck baselines, noisy Boolean sensing). It settles an information-theory design question with the answer 'no clever Boolean function beats forwarding one bit'. Practical demand is modest, since the setting (uniform inputs, BSC noise, one output bit) is stylized.
targets: distributed hypothesis testing / CEO problem one-bit bounds
first_step: Add the proved inequality (with bias refinement) as a citable sharp bound in information-bottleneck/one-bit-compression survey or benchmark docs that currently cite it as conjectural.
caveats: Stylized model with uniform inputs, symmetric noise and a single output bit.

title: Almost-linear-time exact matching and prescribed-degree factors in general graphs
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Finds a maximum-cardinality matching in any graph in (n+m)^{1+o(1)} time with probability 2/3, and likewise finds subgraphs with prescribed vertex degrees (f-factors).
constructive: yes in principle (single uniform algorithm built on almost-linear min-ratio-cycle/flow machinery)
explicit_constants: none: eta(p)->0 'without a convergence rate'; fixed-parameter runs S^{1+O(1/a)+o_a(1)} dovetailed; inherits subpolynomial overheads of Chen et al. almost-linear flow
opportunity: None practical. The o(1) has no rate and the machinery (dynamic min-ratio cycles, routing sparsifiers, flat forests) is the almost-linear max-flow stack that has never been implemented competitively. Production matching codes (LEMON MaxMatching, Boost edmonds_maximum_cardinality_matching, NetworkX, Kolmogorov's Blossom V for weighted) run near-linearly on real sparse graphs already. The O(m log n) Benes-network f-factor reduction is a minor engineering curiosity next to Gabow's direct O(n^{2/3} m) algorithm.
caveats: Not Lean-formalized. It is very long and an extraordinary claim (confidence 2). Even if correct, it is galactic.

title: Almost-linear approximation of edit distance
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: For each fixed eps, a randomized algorithm estimates the edit distance between strings of total length N within factor 1+eps in N^{1+o(1)} expected time.
constructive: yes (uniform algorithm), but below an astronomical threshold it runs the exact quadratic DP
explicit_constants: explicit and absurd: exact DP whenever ell<2^1000, where ell~log2 log2 N, so the approximation branch starts only at N > 2^(2^(2^999)); branching B=H^{p*}, accuracy A_init=H^{p*+4}, tolerances ell^-40, Q1=ell^80; 'thresholds are very large'
opportunity: None. The proposed 'RapidFuzz opt-in approximate API' is baseless: any implementation faithful to the paper executes plain Wagner-Fischer DP on every input that can exist. RapidFuzz already uses bit-parallel Myers/Hyyro exact Levenshtein (O(N*ceil(M/64))). Bioinformatics uses edlib, WFA and banded or seed-and-extend aligners (minimap2), which exploit small distance or structure and beat any worst-case almost-linear scheme on real data.
caveats: Theory resolution of the (1+eps) approximation question. Lean-formalized, but the formal statement is asymptotic ('for all sufficiently large N').
evidence: /root/openai-math/preprints/An-Almost-Linear-Approximation-Scheme-for-Edit-Distance-September-24-2026/build/sections/02-geometry.tex (accuracy-input handling: exact DP if ell<2^1000; parameter block)

title: Quantitative trace-reconstruction bounds with a uniform decoder
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Given independent copies of an unknown n-bit string with each bit randomly deleted, the paper asks how many copies are needed to recover the string exactly. In the worst case n^{Omega(log log n)} copies are required, so a polynomial number is impossible. An explicit decoder recovers the string from quasipolynomially many copies, and from polynomially many when the deletion rate is at most n^{-eps}.
constructive: yes: the decoder fixes one bit at a time and tests each candidate prefix for feasibility of a moment (SDP-type) system in exact rational arithmetic. The lower bound is information-theoretic, built from explicit Thue-Morse-type hard pairs.
explicit_constants: No. Traces <= exp(C*B(n,p)) with B ~ p^-1 log n X^2 (1+log X)^6 and unspecified absolute C, c. The lower-bound exponent c<1/(4 ln 2) holds only asymptotically (q^3 log n -> infinity).
opportunity: The Lean-formalized lower bound settles the polynomial-sample question negatively. Uncoded worst-case reconstruction cannot have polynomial guarantees, so DNA-storage reliability has to come from codebook design (coded trace reconstruction) and average-case behaviour. Practitioners already work this way, so the result confirms practice rather than changing it. The decoder is useless at DNA-storage scale: at n=150 and q=0.01, B(n,p)~351, so the trace budget is exp(351C). Real pipelines use about 10-30 reads per strand with BMA, trellis-BMA, MSA or neural decoders under insertion, deletion and substitution noise.
targets: DNA data-storage decoders (BMA / Trellis-BMA, DNAformer, MSA-based)
coded trace reconstruction / constrained-code design community
first_step: Cite the Lean-formalized lower bound in DNA-storage coding surveys as the formal reason codebooks must exclude worst-case pairs. Optionally brute-force the minimum one-trace TV pairs for n<=24 to check whether Thue-Morse-type pairs already appear at small n and could serve as decoder stress tests.
caveats: Deletion-only channel with a known rate and worst-case inputs. Real strands are coded and random-like, and real channels also have insertions and substitutions. The lower bound holds only in the regime q^3 log n -> infinity. The decoder's polynomial regime q<=n^-eps still has enormous exponents, and CDLSS21 already gave practical-ish polynomial reconstruction for q<=n^{-1/3-eps}.

title: Polynomial-time scheduling on three identical machines
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: This settles Garey-Johnson OPEN8, P3|prec,p_j=1|Cmax: unit-time jobs with arbitrary DAG precedence on exactly three identical machines, no release dates or communication delays. A minimum-makespan schedule can be computed, and deadline feasibility decided, in deterministic polynomial time.
constructive: yes: a dynamic program over polynomially many bounded-size Boolean 'global descriptions' of interval job sets, built from precedence to or from job triples and rank thresholds in a linear extension.
explicit_constants: O((L+2)^150020) multitape steps, with leaf allowance 10000. The authors state that no practical performance claim is made.
opportunity: This settles a famous complexity question but changes nothing for practitioners. Real DAG scheduling, such as compiler instruction scheduling, HPC task graphs, or Sugiyama layer assignment with width 3 (Coffman-Graham ranking), uses list scheduling, Coffman-Graham, CP-SAT or ILP, and these already handle realistic sizes. The remaining channel is research: whether the bounded-global-description decomposition leads to a practical exact DP. It also tells theorists to stop looking for an NP-hardness proof for m=3.
targets: scheduling theory (Nederlof-Swennenhuis-Wegrzycki 2^{O(sqrt n log n)} line)
caveats: Exponent 150020. Covers unit jobs, identical machines and m=3 only; m>=4 is still open. No consequence for weighted or general processing times.

title: The metric k-median approximation threshold and recovery
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Choosing at most k facilities from a candidate list to minimise total client distance can be approximated within 1+2/e+eps, about 1.736, in deterministic polynomial time. This matches the known Max-k-Coverage hardness, so 1+2/e is the exact approximability threshold if P!=NP.
constructive: yes: LP, then grid preparation, iterative directed-graph rounding with an O(1) facility surplus, derandomization, and Li-Svensson surplus removal.
explicit_constants: The hardness constant is explicit. Running time is n^{O(c/eta)} from Li-Svensson enumeration, with grid Delta depending on eps; no explicit exponent is given.
opportunity: This closes the approximability question for k-median with candidate facilities. Practitioners (clustering, facility location, p-median) use local search, Lagrangian or LP heuristics and MIP, which on benchmarks get within a few percent of optimum, so the worst-case factor does not affect them. The only plausibly practical part is the pseudo-approximation stage (LP plus iterative rounding opening k+O(1) facilities) used as an LP-rounding heuristic. The surplus-removal stage is galactic.
caveats: Hardness holds only in the explicit-candidate-facility model; F=J is different. The Li-Svensson enumeration and eps-dependent grid make it impractical. Local search already dominates in practice.

title: Exponential semidefinite complexity of perfect matching
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: No polynomial-size semidefinite program can exactly describe the perfect matching polytope: its PSD rank is 2^{Omega(n)}. This extends Rothvoss's exponential LP extension-complexity bound to SDPs.
constructive: no (lower bound)
explicit_constants: The constant c in 2^{cn} is unspecified; Lean formalizes only superpolynomial growth.
opportunity: None. This belongs to polyhedral and extended-formulation theory. Matching is solved combinatorially (Blossom, LEMON/Blossom V), and no modeler is waiting on compact SDP lifts of the matching polytope.
caveats: Lean formalization covers only the superpolynomial version.

title: Average sensitivity of polynomial threshold functions
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: For the sign of a degree-d polynomial on n Boolean inputs, a random single-bit flip changes the output for at most 8d*sqrt(n) coordinates on average. This gives an explicit O(d sqrt(eta)) noise-sensitivity bound and a uniform-distribution agnostic learner via L1 polynomial regression.
constructive: partial: the bound is structural. The learning corollary is constructive (L1 regression of degree k=O(d^2 alpha^-2 log(1/alpha))).
explicit_constants: yes: 8d sqrt(n); noise sensitivity <= 8 sqrt(2) d sqrt(eta); learner constant A=32*128.
opportunity: This is a learning-theory improvement: it removes Kane's (log n)^{O(d log d)} 2^{O(d^2 log d)} losses for learning PTFs and degree-d sign classifiers under uniform inputs. There is no near-term practical channel. The n^{O(d^2/alpha^2)} learner is impractical, and real feature distributions are not uniform on the cube.
targets: computational learning theory (agnostic learning of PTFs)
caveats: Uniform distribution only. The learner's time n^{k} with k ~ d^2/alpha^2 is impractical.

title: A factor-two approximation for shortest common superstring
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: A deterministic polynomial-time algorithm builds a string containing every input string that is at most twice as long as the shortest possible. Along the way it computes a lower bound W <= OPT from forced substring-occurrence counts, and its output has length <= 2W.
constructive: yes: forced counts m(s) over all substrings (extension rules plus a periodicity rule), a balanced hierarchical graph, decomposition into periodic layers, and connections paid from per-layer budgets, finished with an Euler tour. Fully deterministic.
explicit_constants: The factor 2 is exact. Polynomial degree is not stated; a naive implementation enumerates O(L^2) substrings x periods x shifts x blocking words over V, roughly L^5-L^7 in total input length L.
opportunity: The prior claim that this algorithm should pack zstd dictionary phrases does not hold up. zstd's COVER/FASTCOVER dictionary builders choose segments by dmer-frequency coverage under a byte budget, zero out the frequencies of covered dmers, and memcpy segments end-to-end (legacy ZDICT merges by sample position). The objective is coverage, not shortest superstring, the leftover overlaps are small, and greedy merging would capture them. The more useful artifact is the certificate: W is a polynomially computable lower bound with OPT in [W,2W]. It can certify instance-wise gaps of greedy superstring tools, which are empirically near-optimal even though the Greedy conjecture was disproved (worst case >= 9/4). The natural target is k-mer-set superstrings (KmerCamel masked superstrings, which run greedy on the same hierarchical overlap graph), where inputs have bounded length and W may be tractable.
targets: KmerCamel (masked superstrings / k-mer set representation; global & local greedy on hierarchical overlap graph)
k-mer set compression & SPSS tools (simplitigs, matchtigs, eulertigs) as baselines
first_step: Implement the m(s) recursion (extension rules plus the period rule) with a suffix automaton for fixed-length k-mer inputs, compute W on KmerCamel's benchmark k-mer sets, and report greedy/W ratios against the existing cycle-cover lower bound.
caveats: Lean-formalized and fully constructive, but the period-rule and blocking-functional enumeration is a high-degree polynomial in total length, so naive code is infeasible beyond about L=10^3-10^4. W may be weaker than cycle-cover bounds in practice. The guarantee is worst-case, and greedy already performs well empirically. zstd/ZDICT is not a fit (see opportunity).
evidence: preprints/A-Polynomial-Time-2-Approximation-for-Shortest-Common-Superstring-September-24-2026/build/sections/02-counts.tex (rules eq. extension/period, Lemma counts, Lemma base)

title: Exponential state costs for two-way automata
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Two-way nondeterministic finite automata cannot be complemented with polynomially many states, and one-way NFAs cannot be simulated by two-way DFAs with polynomially many states, when the alphabet is allowed to grow. This resolves the alphabet-growing form of Sakoda-Sipser.
constructive: partial: explicit witness automata; the content is lower bounds.
opportunity: None. Two-way automata are not used in regex engines, model checkers or protocol verifiers, and the separation needs growing alphabets.
caveats: Growing alphabets only; the fixed-alphabet Sakoda-Sipser question remains open.

title: Exact Fourier transforms below n log n
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: A DFT algorithm runs in O(n (log n)^{1-10^-13}) operations at every length, but only in an idealized model: exact complex arithmetic, unbounded coefficients, a supplied root of unity, and no numerical-stability guarantee.
constructive: yes: an explicit uniform algorithm built from a fixed network for tensor powers of C=(1/2)[[1+i,1-i],[1-i,1+i]], a Newton-interpolation local compiler, Good-Thomas CRT axes and a Bluestein chirp.
explicit_constants: yes: m=10^6, W*=2^71, Delta=6871402692000000, theta=1-2.1e-13. The authors say the constants are 'enormous, so these are asymptotic existence and explicitness results, with no useful crossover estimate'.
opportunity: None. The saving factor (log n)^{2e-13} is about 1+10^-12 for any physical n. It is swamped by the (log log n)^4 overhead (about 18-55 at n=2^20-2^64) and by recursion blocks of W*=2^71 arrays. The model also ignores floating-point error. FFTW/genfft, MKL, cuFFT and pocketfft are unaffected; constant-factor work such as split-radix and Alman-Rao-type rigidity savings is the relevant line. The prior mapping of this result to FFTW genfft is a keyword match with no practical basis.
caveats: Exact arithmetic model only, with no bit-complexity or stability claim. The companion nonuniform circuit result is subsequential.

title: Rapid mixing of graph switches for every degree sequence
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: The degree-preserving 'edge swap' random walk, used to generate random networks with the same degrees as an observed one, converges to the uniform distribution in polynomial time for every degree sequence. The lazy version that picks four vertices at random mixes within 2n^8 steps. There is also an exact uniform sampler.
constructive: yes: the chain itself, with explicit Poincare constants, plus an exact sampler based on a rare residual-mixture branch.
explicit_constants: yes: t_mix(1/4) <= 2n^8; spectral gap >= 1/(24 n^2 C(n,4)); Var <= 2n^2 <f,Lf> for the switch-graph Laplacian; H^2 >= H for pair (Curveball) resampling, which implies Var <= sum_a ||h_a f||^2.
opportunity: This removes the standing caveat that switch-chain mixing was proven only for regular, bounded or P-stable degree sequences, a caveat that sits under every configuration-model null model in network science (motif z-scores, rich-club normalization, small-world sigma/omega, modularity nulls). Three concrete consequences follow. (1) Documentation for the NetworkX, igraph, graph-tool and NetworKit swap samplers can cite polynomial mixing for every degree sequence, but only for chains that count rejected proposals as holding steps. (2) NetworkX double_edge_swap and random_reference loop until nswap successful swaps, so their stationary law is proportional to the number of valid swaps, not uniform. An exhaustive check on four small degree sequences gives TV 0.023-0.029 from uniform and max/min probability ratios of 1.25-1.52. (3) Rescaling the paper's Poincare inequality gives explicit budgets that are much better for sparse graphs. A uniform-edge-pair proposal that counts rejections (NetworkX-style, P(G,G')=1/m^2) has gap >= 1/(2n^2 m^2). A random-pair Curveball heat-bath has gap >= 1/C(n,2), which was checked numerically: observed gaps 0.14-0.26 against bounds 0.028-0.048.
targets: NetworkX nx.double_edge_swap / nx.random_reference / nx.rich_club_coefficient(normalized=True) / nx.sigma, nx.omega
Curveball null-model users in ecology/network science (undirected variant; bipartite is FQW26/115)
first_step: Open a NetworkX issue/PR that (a) adds a lazy option counting rejected attempts as steps to double_edge_swap, with a docstring citing the theorem and the 1/(2n^2 m^2) gap, and (b) attaches the exhaustive small-instance bias table.
caveats: Worst-case budgets (2n^8, or about n^2 m^3 log n for edge-pair proposals) are far above the 10-100 swaps per edge used in practice. The result certifies polynomial mixing, not current step counts. It covers simple undirected graphs only; directed and bipartite cases are separate. Connectivity-preserving variants (random_reference) are not covered. The exact sampler is impractical (enumerates the state space on a rare branch). The Lean formalization covers the chain estimates, not the exact sampler. The Curveball-gap and NetworkX-gap corollaries are this triage's own rescaling and need a careful write-up.
evidence: preprints/Polynomial-Mixing-of-the-Switch-Chain-for-Every-Graphical-Degree-Sequence-September-25-2026/build/sections/mixing.tex (Prop mix:global, Cor mix:poincare, Lemma mix:comparison, proof of Thm 1.1)

title: A superquadratic separation of sensitivity and block sensitivity
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: There are total Boolean functions whose block sensitivity exceeds sensitivity^alpha for some alpha>2. This disproves the conjectured quadratic upper bound bs(f) <= O(s(f)^2).
constructive: yes: explicit function family.
explicit_constants: bs/s^2 >= 2^d/(4(d+2)^2); alpha>2 is fixed but not stated numerically.
opportunity: None. This is query-complexity structure theory with no applied channel.

title: The computational complexity of Weisfeiler-Leman refinement
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Deciding whether two graphs are indistinguishable by k-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman refinement needs n^{Omega(k)} time with no complexity assumption, for very large fixed k. When k is part of the input in binary, both equivalence (even on subcubic graphs) and 'does k-WL identify this graph' are EXPTIME-complete.
constructive: partial: explicit hard graph-pair constructions (parity lifts, compressed CFI); the main statements are lower bounds.
explicit_constants: The unconditional bound uses c=c0=1e-9 and needs k large enough that floor(floor(k/1000)/1000) beats the simulation constants (k on the order of 10^6), so the exponent is about 10^-9 k. The ETH-conditional version has unspecified c and K>=4. Parity-lift graph order is A*(t*2^{t-2+3C(t-1,2)}+12C(t,3)), about 10^7*A at k=4 (joint).
opportunity: This is mostly a theory confirmation. GNN expressivity work (k-GNNs, k-WL kernels) already assumes n^k cost is intrinsic; the unconditional bound only covers k on the order of 10^6 and the conditional one has unspecified constants, so practical k=2-3 is untouched. Graph isomorphism tools (nauty, Traces, bliss, saucy) use colour refinement plus individualization and are unaffected. Hard-instance generation for GNN or GI benchmarks such as BREC and CFI suites is impractical: about 10^7 vertices at k=4 joint, about 8000*A vertices at k=4 separate.
targets: GNN expressivity theory (k-WL hierarchy, BREC benchmark)
caveats: The unconditional result applies only at astronomically large k. EXPTIME results need binary-encoded k. Identification hardness does not affect fixed small k.

title: Generalized star height at most three
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Every regular language has a regular expression with complement allowed and at most three nested Kleene stars.
constructive: yes in principle (expression construction via finite-monoid computations), but expressions are huge and size is not controlled.
opportunity: None. Practical regex and automata engines (RE2, Hyperscan, PCRE, automata libraries) do not use complement-based generalized expressions, and expression length is uncontrolled.
caveats: Whether star height <= 1 suffices (the original generalized star-height problem) remains open.

title: Homogeneous depth-five lower bounds for iterated matrix multiplication
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Any homogeneous depth-5 arithmetic circuit computing the (1,1) entry of a product of n generic n-by-n matrices needs n^{Theta(sqrt n)} gates.
constructive: no (lower bound; matching upper construction n^{sqrt n+4})
opportunity: None. This is algebraic circuit complexity (the VP vs VNP program) with no applied channel.

title: A quasilinear PCP theorem for PPAD
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Finding an end of a line in an exponential graph reduces, with only quasilinear blow-up, to finding a point that approximately satisfies all but a constant fraction of the gates of an arithmetic generalized circuit. This is the PCP-for-PPAD conjecture of Babichenko, Papadimitriou and Rubinstein.
constructive: yes (reduction R and decoder D)
explicit_constants: eps, delta are fixed rationals but not stated numerically; size A N ceil(log N)^b.
opportunity: Under ETH-for-PPAD this sharpens lower bounds for constant-approximate two-player Nash and related equilibrium problems toward n^{Omega(log n)}, matching Lipton-Markakis-Mehta. It tells equilibrium-computation and market-design theorists that quasipolynomial support enumeration is essentially optimal. Practical solvers (Gambit, Lemke-Howson, support enumeration, market-clearing heuristics) are unaffected.
targets: algorithmic game theory / equilibrium computation theory
caveats: Hardness consequences still need ETH-for-PPAD. Not Lean-formalized.

title: One-tape time simulation in two-fifths-power space
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: A one-tape Turing machine running for T steps can be simulated with about T^{2/5} space, improving the square-root bound for this model.
constructive: yes (simulator), with unbounded simulation time
opportunity: None. This is a space-time tradeoff in a restricted machine model. The time blow-up is unbounded, so there is no use for memory-constrained computing.
caveats: One writable tape only; multitape is excluded.

title: Subset Sum in O(2^{0.49n}) time
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: This is the first worst-case Subset Sum algorithm (n integers of polynomially many bits) with running-time exponent below the 50-year-old meet-in-the-middle 2^{n/2}: 2^{0.49n}, randomized with bounded error. A companion paper keeps 2^{n/2} time but uses only 2^{n/5} memory.
constructive: yes: a randomized algorithm combining isolation, a filtered Fourier 'checksum' estimate with a random prime modulus, and representation-method enumeration of modular aliases.
explicit_constants: Intermediate bound 2^{0.489995n} poly(n+b+2), with an unspecified polynomial. Parameters eta=.51772, tau=.48996, gamma=.48925 come from numerical certificates. The low-space variant has an (n+b+2)^15 2^{0.199n} space factor.
opportunity: There is no cryptographic consequence. Knapsack and subset-sum cryptanalysis is average-case at density ~1, where representation methods (HGJ, BCJ, BBSS) already reach about 2^{0.28-0.29n}, and deployed lattice schemes (Kyber/ML-KEM, Dilithium/ML-DSA) are parameterized by lattice attacks, not worst-case Subset Sum. The 0.01n exponent gain only beats Horowitz-Sahni once 2^{0.01n} exceeds the polynomial overhead, around n~2*10^4 for an n^15-type factor, where both are astronomically infeasible. The real effect is on fine-grained complexity: the hypothesis that worst-case Subset Sum needs 2^{n/2} time is refuted, and reductions that assume it must be rechecked.
targets: fine-grained complexity hypothesis lists (Subset Sum / k-SUM style lower-bound assumptions)
caveats: Not Lean-formalized. The argument is long and relies on numerical certificates. Worst-case only, randomized. The 2^{0.49n} constant absorbs a polynomial using only 2^{0.000005n} slack, so constants are enormous.

title: Subpolynomial query complexity for log-concave sampling
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: To draw an approximate sample (TV 1/10) from exp(-V) on R^d when V is smooth and very well conditioned (I <= Hessian <= 2I) with a known minimizer, C_eps d^eps gradient evaluations suffice for every eps>0, and at least about log d are needed. So the dimension exponent of gradient-query cost is zero.
constructive: partial: an explicit measurable algorithm (high-order Picard/collocation flows with recursive noisy conditional means), but with unbounded real computation between queries and eps-dependent approximation orders.
explicit_constants: No. C_eps is unspecified, presumably enormous for small eps, and no arithmetic-cost bound is given. The lower bound c log d also has an unspecified c.
opportunity: This redirects sampling theory rather than software. It shows that the d^{1/3} (shifted composition) to d^{1/6}-d^{1/5} (Picard, cloud) gradient-query barriers are not intrinsic, so the research target is practical high-order samplers whose gradient cost grows very slowly with dimension. Bayesian software (Stan NUTS, PyMC, NumPyro, BlackJAX) is unaffected. Its targets have condition numbers far above 2, the query count ignores computation between queries, and C_eps is unquantified.
caveats: Condition number <=2, known minimizer, exact gradients, fixed TV 1/10. Oracle complexity only: arbitrary real computation between queries is free.

title: Memory-sample lower bounds for noiseless Gaussian regression
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: A one-pass learner that keeps at most A*d^2 bits between exact Gaussian linear measurements needs Omega(d log(1/eps)) measurements to recover a unit vector to angle eps. Extra memory at constant precision does not reduce the number of samples below what Kaczmarz or SGD already uses.
constructive: no (lower bound; Kaczmarz shows tightness with real registers)
explicit_constants: Partly: 2^{-16} d log2(1/eps) for o(d^2) memory (subsphere paper); c_A unspecified for A d^2 memory.
opportunity: This certifies that streaming Kaczmarz/SGD-type regression, at O(d log 1/eps) samples with O(d) words of memory, is sample-optimal among learners with subquadratic or constant-precision quadratic memory. The audience is memory- or quantization-constrained streaming least squares (on-device learning, sketch-and-solve). It gives a formal reason not to spend memory budget on partial Gram or sketch states expecting fewer samples. It is a clean theoretical certificate, but no practitioner decision currently depends on it.
targets: streaming / online least-squares theory (randomized Kaczmarz, SGD)
caveats: Noiseless Gaussian design, uniform spherical prior, and fixed A only. It does not cover d^2 log(1/eps) bits, which is what RLS uses to solve in d samples.
evidence: preprints/Memory-and-precision-in-noiseless-Gaussian-regression-September-27-2026/build/sections/introduction.tex (Def h:model, Thm h:main, Cors, Kaczmarz benchmark)

title: Existential-universal real sentences in the counting hierarchy
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: Deciding whether a system of polynomial equations and inequalities has a real solution (the existential theory of the reals), and even one exists-forall alternation, can be done in a fixed level of the counting hierarchy (ETR in C_26), which is well inside PSPACE.
constructive: partial (complexity-class membership; no practical procedure)
explicit_constants: ETR in counting level 26; level j for exists-forall unspecified.
opportunity: None in practice. SMT solvers for nonlinear real arithmetic (z3 nlsat, cvc5, Yices2 MCSat, QEPCAD/CAD) are unaffected, and exists-R-complete problems such as neural-network training and art gallery stay as hard as before. This is a structural complexity refinement inside PSPACE.
caveats: Not Lean-formalized.

title: Deterministic polynomial factorization over prime fields
subject: Theoretical computer science
plain_english: This gives the first deterministic, GRH-free algorithm that factors any degree-n polynomial over F_p in time polynomial in n and log p. Randomized Cantor-Zassenhaus has done this in expected polynomial time since 1981.
constructive: yes: Berlekamp algebra, then a separating element, then even-degree tournament splitting with a 2-primary generator or odd-degree splitting via cyclic curves Y^q=F(X), lambda-division in Jacobians and norm equations in cyclic algebras. Auxiliary primes l are found by upward search.
explicit_constants: Bit cost O(((n+1)ceil(log2 p))^{10^12}); refined O(B^{400000100}) with B=20+(n+1)(L+1). The algebraic part is O(B^{500000}+B^{100}E^{20}), where E is the largest auxiliary prime, guaranteed <= c0 B^{2*10^7} via a zero-free strip delta=1e-6. The large-characteristic machinery runs only for p>B^{200000}, i.e. primes of at least ~4.8 million bits even at n=2. Every smaller p uses Berlekamp with exhaustive scalar search costing about p trials.
opportunity: This is not practical against Cantor-Zassenhaus. CZ, Kaltofen-Shoup and Kedlaya-Umans run in expected roughly O~(n^2 log p) or n^{1.5+o(1)} log p field operations, and their output is Las Vegas and checkable (product plus irreducibility tests), so randomness never threatens correctness. For every prime anyone uses (up to a few thousand bits), the algorithm falls into its small-characteristic branch, which is deterministic Berlekamp with exhaustive search, i.e. exponential in log p. The one action is REDIRECT: once refereed, textbook and library-doc statements that deterministic polynomial-time factoring is open need updating. FLINT, NTL, SymPy and PARI should not implement it. The algebraic reduction alone also gives the first GRH-conditional deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, improving Evdokimov's quasipolynomial bound.
targets: von zur Gathen-Gerhard 'Modern Computer Algebra' ch. 14 notes
first_step: Do not implement. Record in CAS documentation and survey notes that deterministic polynomial-time factorization over F_p is claimed, flagging that it depends on the unformalized companion Hecke zero-free theorem (family 029).
caveats: The unconditional claim rests on an extraordinary, unformalized analytic input: a uniform zero-free strip of width 1e-6 for all finite-order Hecke L-functions over cyclotomic fields containing mu_12 (companion 029). Exponent 10^12. Determinism has no practical value because CZ output is verifiable.

title: A counterexample to periodic tiling in dimension three
subject: Combinatorics
plain_english: There is a finite set of cubes in 3D that can tile space by translations but never in a repeating (periodic) pattern; it is the first such example in the lowest possible dimension.
constructive: yes (finite tile selected by terminating finite searches; size not bounded)
explicit_constants: none; paper says 'no practical bound on the size of the finite construction'
opportunity: No applied channel. The only CS-relevant consequence is theoretical: 'search for a periodic tiling' is not a complete decision procedure for translational monotile tiling in Z^3 (consistent with Greenfeld-Tao undecidability work). The tile is astronomically large and has no materials/quasicrystal relevance.
caveats: Tile size unbounded; translational-only setting.
evidence: 07-three-dimensions.tex remark 'Finite selection of the tile data'

title: Borsuk's conjecture fails in dimension nine
subject: Combinatorics
plain_english: The set of all rank-one projection matrices for lines in R^4 (a 9-dimensional object) cannot be split into 10 pieces of smaller diameter, so Borsuk's conjecture fails already in dimension 9 (previous record 63).
constructive: yes (explicit compact set; obstruction is topological)
opportunity: No applied channel. The set is the space of real pure qubit-pair-like projectors and the proof uses orthogonality colourings reminiscent of Kochen-Specker arguments, but nothing transfers to quantum contextuality tests or clustering practice.
caveats: Continuous (not finite) counterexample; no benchmark value.

title: Graph coloring, clique minors, and Colin de Verdière invariants
subject: Combinatorics
plain_english: Hadwiger's famous conjecture (chromatic number <= largest clique minor) is false, even fractionally; but list-chromatic number is at most a universal constant times the Hadwiger number.
constructive: partial (counterexamples sampled from a finite probability space with huge fixed parameters; list bound existential with unspecified C=2(Q+6K))
explicit_constants: counterexample ratio h<26m/75; list constant C not numerically given
opportunity: No benchmark value for colouring solvers: the counterexamples have independence number <=2, and colouring such graphs is polynomial (chi = m - maximum matching of the complement), so they are trivial for DSATUR/SAT colourers. Computing Hadwiger number is hard but nobody benchmarks it. The linear list-colouring bound has an unspecified constant and no algorithm.
caveats: Random construction with very large M_0; Colin de Verdiere and fractional parts not Lean-checked.

title: The Euclidean plane cannot be colored with five colors
subject: Combinatorics
plain_english: Any 5-colouring of the plane has two points at distance 1 with the same colour, so the chromatic number of the plane is 6 or 7.
constructive: no (via de Bruijn-Erdos compactness a finite non-5-colourable unit-distance graph exists, but it is not exhibited and its size is unbounded)
explicit_constants: none for the finite witness; badness constant delta=1/|E(H)| existential
opportunity: Non-obvious channel: the SAT community (Heule's 509-553 vertex 5-chromatic unit-distance graphs, Polymath16) has been searching for a finite unit-distance graph needing 6 colours; this proves one exists, so SAT/cube-and-conquer searches for it are no longer potentially futile. If found, it would be a famous hard UNSAT benchmark. The proof gives no size bound, so the witness may be far beyond SAT reach.
first_step: Post to the Polymath16/SAT-search community that a finite 6-chromatic UDG is now guaranteed; ask whether the proof's Moser-spindle placement step suggests a candidate vertex set.
caveats: Existence only; witness could be astronomically large.

title: Erdős’s reciprocal-sum conjecture and quasipolynomial Szemerédi bounds
subject: Combinatorics
plain_english: Any set of integers whose reciprocals sum to infinity contains arithmetic progressions of every length; quantitatively, progression-free subsets of {1..N} are smaller than N/exp((log N)^eps_k).
constructive: n/a (upper bound / density statement)
explicit_constants: C_k,c_k,eps_k unspecified; only the qualitative reciprocal-sum statement is Lean-checked
opportunity: No applied channel. Upper bounds on AP-free sets constrain, but do not help, Behrend/Salem-Spencer-type constructions used in matrix-multiplication and NOF-communication arguments; practical algorithms are unaffected.
caveats: Quantitative part not formalized.

title: Superexponential van der Waerden numbers
subject: Combinatorics
plain_english: Proves van der Waerden numbers grow faster than any exponential: W_r(k) > k^{c k floor(log2 r)}.
constructive: partial (random perturbed-ellipsoid colouring with LLL; K_0 non-explicit)
opportunity: No applied channel. Blunt check: for r=2 the bound k^{1e-5 k} beats Berlekamp's elementary p*2^p only when log2 k > 1e5, i.e. k > 2^100000, so SAT-based exact computations of small W(r,k) (the only practical activity here) gain nothing.
caveats: Galactic crossover vs classical constructions.

title: Counterexamples to Sidorenko’s conjecture and the forcing conjecture
subject: Combinatorics
plain_english: A specific 35-vertex, 66-edge bipartite graph appears less often in some graph than in a random graph of the same density, so Sidorenko's conjecture is false; matching its count and the edge density also does not force a graph to look random.
constructive: partial (pattern H explicit: incidence graph of 22 triples on 13 points; host G only shown to exist by sampling a kernel)
explicit_constants: H explicit; host size not given
opportunity: Faint STAT/network-science channel: subgraph-count tests for quasirandomness cannot rely on this H's density (forcing fails), but practical tests use C4 counts (Chung-Graham-Wilson), which remain valid. No practical change.
caveats: Only the Sidorenko part is Lean-checked; host graph existential.

title: Counterexamples to Ryser’s covering conjecture
subject: Combinatorics
plain_english: Builds intersecting r-partite hypergraphs needing r vertices to cover all edges, refuting Ryser's predicted r-1 (for r = q+1, q a large prime), and refutes Gyarfas's tree-cover conjecture.
constructive: partial (algebraic/probabilistic constructions; prime thresholds existential)
opportunity: No applied channel.
caveats: Existential thresholds.

title: Hindman’s finite sums and products conjecture
subject: Combinatorics
plain_english: In any finite colouring of the positive integers there are k-element sets whose subset sums and subset products all share one colour.
constructive: no (Ramsey-type existence)
opportunity: No applied channel.
caveats: Unformalized.

title: The Harary–Hill and Zarankiewicz crossing-number formulas
subject: Combinatorics
plain_english: The minimum number of edge crossings when drawing the complete graph K_n, and the complete bipartite graph K_{m,n}, in the plane is exactly the classical conjectured formula (e.g. ~n^4/64 for K_n), proved for all n.
constructive: yes (matching two-page / axis drawings are explicit; lower bound is an algebraic rank argument)
opportunity: Non-obvious channels checked: (1) single-layer photonic all-to-all waveguide meshes and graph-drawing benchmarks now have certified exact optima for K_n (previously exact only to n=14) and K_{m,n}; but the asymptotic lower bound was already within 1.5% (Balogh-Lidicky-Salazar 0.9856), and no heuristic ever beat Hill's drawing, so practice does not change. (2) VLSI area lower bounds use crossing number via Leighton, but multilayer VLSI crossings are free, and straight-line (rectilinear) drawings have a different, larger crossing number that this result does not settle. Real value: CERTIFY reference data (OEIS A000241, crossing-number surveys, OGDF/KnownCR benchmark ground truth) and RESEARCH reuse of the polynomial-interpolation lower-bound method for open cases (complete tripartite, hypercube Q_n).
first_step: Submit an OEIS edit marking A000241 (and the Zarankiewicz sequence) proved for all n, citing the Lean-checked theorem.
caveats: Ordinary (curved-arc) crossing number only, not rectilinear; practical design decisions unchanged.
evidence: WebSearch: no ONoC literature uses cr(K_n) as a bound

title: The higher-dimensional Erdős distinct-distances conjecture
subject: Combinatorics
plain_english: n points in d-dimensional space (d>=3) always determine at least c_d n^{2/d} distinct distances, which is optimal up to the constant.
constructive: n/a

title: Planar distinct distances and unit-distance bounds
subject: Combinatorics

constructive: n/a

title: Combinatorial invariance of Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials
subject: Combinatorics

constructive: no (invariance via moment-graph sheaves; no algorithm computing P from the poset)
opportunity: Faint CAS channel: in large KL computations (Coxeter3, SageMath KazhdanLusztigPolynomial, Atlas of Lie Groups) one could in principle memoize P by the isomorphism class of the interval poset, but poset-isomorphism testing is likely costlier than the standard recursion. Also validates the DeepMind ML-guided conjecture programme (Davies-Williamson et al.), a meta-point for AI-for-math rather than an applied action.

title: Deterministic construction of strong thin spanning trees
subject: Combinatorics
plain_english: Every k-edge-connected multigraph has a spanning tree that uses at most a C/k fraction of every cut, and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm finds it. This is the 'thin tree' object behind one route to approximating asymmetric TSP.

The thin-and-cheap rounding corollary resolves AGMOS Conjecture 6.1 with (24B,24B) constants, giving an O(1) ATSP algorithm with an unknown, enormous constant. The algorithm is non-trivial only for astronomically large connectivity (r^{-1/16} losses need a huge R_0), so it is galactic. Practical ATSP (LKH-3, Concorde via symmetric transform, OR-Tools) is unaffected. Remaining value is theory: the MSS-type sparsification with packing preservation may be reusable in network-design rounding (survivable network design, low-congestion spanning trees).

title: Bounded-degree coboundary expanders
subject: Combinatorics
plain_english: Constructs high-dimensional 'expander' simplicial complexes (generalizations of expander graphs to triangles, tetrahedra, etc.) with bounded degree and strong mod-2 coboundary expansion in all dimensions below d, for every d.

Value is theoretical: it may unlock new agreement tests or codes from higher-dimensional cochains.

title: Deterministic nonbipartite Ramanujan graphs in every fixed degree
subject: Combinatorics
plain_english: For every degree d>=3, a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm outputs a d-regular graph on any large even number of vertices whose nontrivial eigenvalues all lie strictly within the optimal Ramanujan bound 2*sqrt(d-1); these are optimal spectral expanders.
constructive: yes (deterministic, poly(n) bit operations; outputs full adjacency list, not a local neighbour oracle)
explicit_constants: exponent k_d and n_0(d) unspecified; internal scales such as girth exclusion q^{g_0} ~ n^{0.002a} with a = 1e-4 (i.e. n^{2e-7}) must dominate fixed constants, so n_0(d) is astronomically large (n^{2e-7} >= 2 already needs n >= 2^{5,000,000}); the repair stage also enumerates Bernstein approximations of degree n^{2(c+C)}
opportunity: Checked the expander/LDPC/derandomization channels. (a) Practice: random d-regular graphs are Ramanujan with limiting probability ~0.69 (Huang-McKenzie-Yau), so 'sample, then verify' (NetworkX random_regular_expander_graph, which loops over maybe_regular_expander_graph and checks with is_regular_expander) is already an expected O(1)-trial Las Vegas method at real sizes; this algorithm is galactic. (b) Derandomization needs strongly explicit expanders (local neighbour queries), which the paper explicitly does not provide. (c) LDPC/expander codes use PEG / quasi-cyclic designs and do not require exact Ramanujan spectra. The paper's one practical by-product: exact certification of the Ramanujan property via rational inertia of B^T(4(d-1)I - A^2)B with B = [e_i - e_n], which could replace floating-point eigsh checks.
first_step: Optional small IMPLEMENT: propose an exact=True mode for networkx.is_regular_expander using the paper's exact test (an LDL^T inertia check of 4(d-1)B^TB - (AB)^T(AB)) for small graphs; low priority.
caveats: Galactic; unformalized; 6.4k lines of delicate analysis; strongly explicit constructions (LPS/Morgenstern) remain the only usable deterministic ones in restricted degrees.

title: The circulant Hadamard and Barker-sequence conjectures
subject: Combinatorics
plain_english: Proves that +/-1 circulant Hadamard matrices (equivalently, binary sequences with perfectly zero periodic autocorrelation) exist only for lengths 1 and 4, and hence that binary Barker codes (peak sidelobe 1) exist only at lengths 2,3,4,5,7,11,13: no Barker code longer than 13 exists.
constructive: yes (nonexistence proof; witnesses for n=1,4 explicit)
opportunity: Yes, it settles the radar/sonar/spread-spectrum question: the even case is closed by the circulant Hadamard theorem and the odd case by Turyn-Storer (1961). It also proves no binary sequence of length > 4 has ideal periodic autocorrelation. Bluntly, practice will not change: Logan-Mossinghoff-type computations had already excluded every length 13 < n <= 4e33 except one (n ~ 3.98e33), and designers already use Barker-13, nested Barker, MPS-optimized binary codes, m-sequences or polyphase/Zadoff-Chu codes. The concrete actions are certification: update references that still say 'conjectured' (radar textbooks, Wikipedia, OEIS), close residual computational searches, and upstream the Lean proof to Mathlib.
targets: Radar pulse-compression references (Levanon & Mozeson 'Radar Signals'; Richards 'Fundamentals of Radar Signal Processing'; Skolnik)
first_step: Upstream OAI/LinearAlgebra/CirculantHadamard (exists_iff_order_one_or_four) and the even-Barker lemma to Mathlib, then update OEIS/Wikipedia with the Lean-verified citation.
caveats: Lean covers the circulant Hadamard theorem and the even-Barker part only; the odd Barker classification relies on the classical Turyn-Storer proof. Several earlier claimed proofs were false, but the Lean check mitigates this. Engineering decisions are unchanged.

title: Barnette’s Hamiltonian-cycle conjecture
subject: Combinatorics
plain_english: Every 3-connected cubic bipartite planar graph has a Hamiltonian cycle (a tour visiting each vertex once); moreover the cycle can avoid any chosen edge.

opportunity: Two modest channels. (2) RESEARCH: the search problem becomes total (TFNP-like). The proof's sum Z(x) is a signed sum over matching-like 'state pairs' on a planar triangulation with Pfaffian structure, so asking whether Z or a self-reducible variant is computable by Kasteleyn/Pfaffian determinants is a concrete route to a polynomial-time algorithm.
targets: FHCP Challenge Set / Concorde HCP benchmarks
first_step: Check whether the exponential sum Z(x) over state pairs factors as a determinant/Pfaffian (Kasteleyn-Temperley correspondence noted in the paper); if so, self-reduction gives a poly-time Hamiltonian-cycle algorithm for this class.
caveats: Existence only; HCP on this class may already be easy in practice for heuristics.

title: The quasi-Riemann hypothesis
subject: Number theory
plain_english: No Dirichlet L-function (including zeta) has a zero with real part > 7/8, and there are no Landau-Siegel zeros. Consequently the least quadratic non-residue mod p is at most C(log p)^A, so square roots mod p (deterministic Tonelli-Shanks) and Miller's primality test run in deterministic polynomial time without GRH.

Landau-Siegel constant c is not explicit (proof by contradiction). Cor. PNT in APs with error x^{11/12} log x, effective but not explicit.
opportunity: This is a certification result, not a software one. Textbook and complexity statements become unconditional: 'square roots mod p, deterministic poly time (was GRH)', Vinogradov's n(p)<<p^eps, effective h(D)>>sqrt|D|/loglog|D|, and effective PNT in progressions; Galbraith §2.9, Cohen, Crandall-Pomerance, Shoup and Wikipedia can drop the GRH caveat. In practice nothing changes. (log p)^16..32 is about 10^46..10^91 at 1024 bits. It beats the unconditional Burgess bound p^0.152 only above roughly 1000 bits (about 2200 bits for the paper's A=32), and that is before the uncomputed constant C, while OpenSSL BN_mod_sqrt tries at most ~80 candidates and FLINT n_quadratic_nonresidue scans. AKS/Lenstra-Pomerance is already better than a deterministic Miller test. KEY NEGATIVE: the GRH dependence in PARI bnfinit/quadclassunit/bnfisnorm, Magma ClassGroup Proof:="GRH", Sage proof=False and CSI-FiSh's CSIDH-512 class group concerns Hecke L-functions of class-group characters of K, not Dirichlet L-functions. 003 does not cover them (only K=Q(sqrt-3)), so those caveats must stay.

The corollaries are classical implications and are not formalized. The 11/12 alternate proof is independent. All algorithmic consequences are galactic.

subject: Number theory

title: The ordinary-double-point volume gap
subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
plain_english: Proves that every singular klt singularity of dimension n has 'normalized volume' at most 2(n-1)^n. The maximum is achieved only by the ordinary double point (the cone z_0^2+...+z_n^2=0).
constructive: n/a (sharp inequality with characterized equality)
opportunity: Physics corollary, of curiosity value only. For Calabi–Yau cones with a Ricci-flat metric, normalized volume equals n^n·Vol(L)/Vol(S^{2n-1}) for the Sasaki–Einstein link L (Martelli–Sparks–Yau, Li–Liu–Xu). The new n=4 case therefore says every Sasaki–Einstein 7-manifold other than round S^7 has volume ≤ Vol(V_{5,2}) = (81/128)Vol(S^7). In AdS4/CFT3, F_{S^3} ∝ N^{3/2}Vol^{-1/2}, which gives a universal large-N free-energy gap F ≥ sqrt(128/81)·F_{S^7} ≈ 1.257·F_{S^7} for M2-brane SCFTs with non-maximally-supersymmetric Sasaki–Einstein duals. The n=3 (AdS5, conifold/T^{1,1}) case was already known (Liu–Xu 2019). Only hep-th theorists benefit; no computation changes.
first_step: Write a one-page note stating the SE7 volume gap and the F_{S^3} gap, and check it against the tabulated SE7 volumes (V_{5,2}, Q^{111}, M^{111}, N^{010}, toric families).
caveats: Unformalized, though it builds on established normalized-volume theory and the dimension-4 base case is a separate companion paper. The physics translation assumes the Ricci-flat cone exists (K-polystable), which holds for Sasaki–Einstein links by definition. Known volumes (Q^{111}=π^4/8, M^{111}=9π^4/128) are consistent with the bound V_{5,2}=27π^4/128.

title: Nagata’s conjecture and maximal Seshadri constants
subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
plain_english: Proves Nagata's conjecture: a plane curve of degree d through r ≥ 10 very general points with multiplicities m_i satisfies Σm_i < d·sqrt(r). Equivalently, the r-point Seshadri constant of P^2 is 1/sqrt(r). Also shows multipoint Seshadri constants are maximal for large r on any polarized variety.
constructive: no: degeneration argument at very general points; certifies no explicit configuration
explicit_constants: explicit (sqrt r) for Nagata; r_0(X,L) non-explicit for higher-dim Seshadri
opportunity: None after checking the three channels that were asked about. (1) Splines/interpolation: through inverse systems (Emsalem–Iarrobino, Geramita–Schenck), trivariate C^r spline dimension on a vertex star with s interior faces involves R/(ℓ_i^{r+1}), which is dual to fat points of multiplicity d−r in P^2. Nagata only says this vanishes for d ≥ r·sqrt(s)/(sqrt(s)−1). For practical smoothness (r ≤ 2) that is trivial, because s ≥ 10 generic powers already span R_{r+1}. In general, Nagata adds nothing for m ≤ 11, where SHGH was already verified (Dumnicki–Jarnicki). Spline and Hermite poisedness questions need SHGH non-speciality, not Nagata. Real meshes and grids are not 'very general': my mod-p check found nonzero systems throughout the Nagata range for points on a conic. (2) AG codes: Hansen's bound d ≥ n − L^2/e uses the Seshadri constant at the F_q-rational evaluation points. Those are maximally special, and the char-p result is only at the geometric generic (transcendental) tuple, so no code bound improves. (3) The Waldschmidt constant (Macaulay2 SymbolicPowers 'waldschmidt') equals sqrt(r) only for very general points and certifies nothing for a given rational point set.
caveats: Top line is Lean-formalized (OAI.Nagata.nagata_conjecture; the PlaneCurves dir has no sorry/axiom). The large-r Seshadri threshold r_0(X,L) is non-explicit (Lean doc). The 'very general' hypothesis means a countable union of exceptional loci, so no specific configuration is certified.

For beta>1 it stays far from equilibrium for stretched-exponential time when started from a typical equilibrium state.

Constants are implicit, the results hold in probability over Gaussian disorder at zero field, and the low-temperature barriers are galactic, so no practitioner changes burn-in or ladder design.

title: Exact three- and four-state reconstruction thresholds and four-state tree capacity
subject: Probability and statistical mechanics
plain_english: When a 3-state (either sign) or assortative 4-state symbol is broadcast down a tree through a noisy symmetric channel, the root can be recovered from far-away leaves exactly when d·lambda^2>1 (the Kesten–Stigum bound), for every degree. Consequently, 3 symmetric communities in a sparse stochastic block model can be weakly recovered iff (a-b)^2 > 3(a+2b).
constructive: partial: the impossibility side is information-theoretic, and achievability reuses the existing O(n log n) Abbe–Sandon algorithm. The proofs are computer-assisted, with exact-arithmetic C++/Python verifiers shipped.
explicit_constants: Yes: the thresholds are exact (d·lambda^2=1; SBM (a-b)^2=3(a+2b)).
opportunity: This certifies at every average degree the KS reference line that community-detection benchmarks (BP, non-backtracking spectral, line-graph GNN papers) plot against for q=3; previously only large degree was proven (Mossel–Sly–Sohn 2025). Non-obvious BIO channel: the ferromagnetic 4-state channel is exactly the Jukes–Cantor substitution model. The root (ancestral) state of a deep d-ary tree, including binary trees, is therefore unrecoverable exactly when per-branch change probability p >= (3/4)(1-1/sqrt d), about 0.22 for d=2. This pins the KS phase transition used in phylogenetic sequence-length theory. Both uses confirm what practitioners already assumed.
targets: community-detection benchmark suites and papers using SBM KS threshold curves
phylogenetic reconstruction theory (Jukes–Cantor ancestral reconstruction / sequence-length phase transitions)
first_step: Cite the exact q=3 SBM threshold (and the q=4 assortative tree threshold) as the proven reference line in SBM benchmark generators and surveys. Note in phylogenetics theory surveys that KS-sharpness for Jukes–Cantor on regular and Poisson trees is now a (computer-assisted) theorem.
caveats: Lean formalizes only the classical supercritical direction. The new non-reconstruction direction is unformalized and computer-assisted. The 4-state result is tree-only; an assortative 4-community SBM corollary likely follows via the same transfer but is not stated. Equal branch lengths and equal-size communities only.

title: The free uniform spanning forest is a factor of IID
subject: Probability and statistical mechanics
plain_english: The free uniform spanning forest on any infinite graph can be generated from independent per-vertex random labels by one symmetric rule that needs no root. The same holds for invariant strongly Rayleigh and determinantal processes on countable groups.
constructive: no: Borel and non-finitary (Brownian-path/SDE readout via limsups), with no coding radius
opportunity: None. The construction reads out a limsup of infinitely many Brownian paths and has no finitary coding radius, so it gives no local or parallel sampler. Practical spanning-tree and DPP sampling (Wilson's algorithm, spectral DPP samplers) is untouched.
caveats: Infinite graphs and groups only.
